claims.text: Controlled substrate preheating during additive manufacturing of high-entropy alloys reduces thermal gradients between the melt pool and substrate.
Reduced thermal gradients improve the dimensional precision of additively manufactured high-entropy-alloy components.
Reduced thermal gradients improve the mechanical integrity of additively manufactured high-entropy-alloy components.
Controlled substrate preheating reduces fabrication-induced defects relative to room-temperature builds.
Preheating promotes a more uniform temperature distribution during fabrication.
A more uniform temperature distribution minimizes thermal stresses caused by rapid cooling.
Minimizing rapid-cooling-induced thermal stresses reduces porosity.
Minimizing rapid-cooling-induced thermal stresses reduces cracking.
Reducing fabrication-induced defects enhances dimensional precision.
Reducing fabrication-induced defects enhances mechanical integrity.
Substrate preheating between 200°C and 500°C under inert-atmosphere selective laser melting will produce measurable improvements in dimensional accuracy relative to room-temperature processing.
Substrate preheating between 200°C and 500°C under inert-atmosphere selective laser melting will improve tensile strength and ductility relative to room-temperature processing.
The magnitude of improvement may vary among high-entropy-alloy compositions.
The magnitude of improvement may vary with substrate preheat temperature.
